title: Not my judgment
hook: the tyrant has power over the body, never the judgment (Discourses 1.19)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the clay lamp, and your line, a clay lamp. Was there something small you let go of? Day four hundred three.

Epictetus' old master, Epaphroditus, once sold a slave who made shoes, because he thought the man was useless. Then the shoemaker was bought by someone in the emperor's household and became the emperor's own shoemaker. Suddenly Epaphroditus couldn't do enough for him. How is our dear Felicio, he'd ask. And if you came looking for Epaphroditus, you'd be told he was in a meeting with Felicio. Epictetus tells this story with a straight face, and it's devastating. Today: not my judgment.
screen: `THE USELESS SHOEMAKER.` → `NOW HE WORKS FOR THE EMPEROR.` → `IN A MEETING WITH FELICIO.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book one, chapter nineteen: how we should behave toward tyrants. Felicio is the joke that opens the door. Why did Epaphroditus suddenly fawn over his old shoemaker? Not because Felicio changed. Because Felicio was now near power, and Epaphroditus wanted what power gives. Epictetus says that's how we all get pushed around. Nobody, he says, really fears the emperor himself. They fear what he can do: death, exile, prison, the loss of their property. And nobody loves him for himself either. They love the money and the posts he hands out. So whoever controls the things you want or dread is your master. Then the tyrant speaks. I'll chain you. I'll take your property. Do it, the student of Epictetus says. Those were never fully mine. But your judgment, what you consider good and bad, what you agree to, what you choose: no one can reach in and change it. They can threaten. They can make choosing costly. But the choosing stays with you. Tyrants come in small sizes, too: a boss who controls your schedule, a relative who controls the family's approval, an online crowd that controls how you feel about yourself. Epictetus' question works on all of them. What exactly can they touch? Your paycheck, maybe. Your mood, only if you hand it over. Your judgment: never. That's not a promise that standing firm will be painless. It's a map of where the fight actually is.
screen: `WHY FAWN OVER FELICIO?` · `WE FEAR WHAT POWER CAN DO.` · `THE TYRANT CAN'T REACH THE JUDGMENT.` · `TYRANTS IN SMALL SIZES.` · then, large: `NOT MY JUDGMENT.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Name one fear that's been pressing on you lately: losing a job, someone's disapproval, a diagnosis, money. Say it plainly to yourself. Now sort it. What could this actually touch? Write the list in your mind: my income, my plans, my comfort, my body. Then name what it can't touch: what I value, how I treat people, whether I stay honest. Rest your attention on that second list for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Not my judgment. Epictetus to the tyrant: you can chain the body and take the property, but you can't reach the judgment.
Your line: not my judgment. When someone with power over you leans on you today, ask quietly what they can touch, and remind yourself: not my judgment. Day four hundred three.

howItsDone: Stoic readers often sort a fear into what it could touch and what it can't, keeping their attention on their own judgment and choices.

fork.setup: the tyrant says: I'll chain you and take your property. you're a student of Epictetus. what's your answer?
options: do it; those were never fully mine, and my judgment you can't touch.
fork.reveal: the student lets go of what was never fully his, and keeps the one thing no tyrant can reach: judgment.

original.note: Greek dogma: a judgment or settled opinion; Epictetus uses it for the views that shape our reactions.

trapdoor: what you thought: no one can tell me what to do.
what it means: power can reach your body and property, but never your judgment of good and bad.
what a scholar hears: the Felicio anecdote is one of the few glimpses of Epictetus' own household; his old master Epaphroditus was a freedman of Nero.
